conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hi, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you tonight. Can you tell me what brought you to the hospital?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi… I’ve been feeling really sick. I was having trouble breathing and felt super weak. My blood sugar was really high when I checked it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. The ER team told me your blood sugar was 824 and you weren’t making insulin. You’ve had DKA before, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes… I know. I haven’t been taking my insulin. I missed a few days. I was sick with a cold and just didn’t feel like doing it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But stopping insulin, even when you're sick, can be dangerous. Your body starts breaking down fat, which makes acids build up—called ketoacidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know, I just… didn’t think it would get this bad. I didn’t mean to hurt myself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We don’t think you did. But the team wanted to make sure you’re safe, so psychiatry will check in with you tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I’m not suicidal. I just get overwhelmed sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good to hear. Right now, we’re treating your DKA with an insulin drip and fluids. Your potassium was high when you came in—7.1—but it’s coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: High potassium? I thought diabetics usually have low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good question. Usually yes, but in DKA, acidosis can push potassium out of cells, making it high at first. We gave you calcium gluconate to protect your heart.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… that makes sense. My kidneys were off too, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your creatinine was 1.7, which means your kidneys were stressed from dehydration. But with fluids, it’s already down to 1.1. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been so dry. My mouth feels like sand.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s from being dehydrated. We’re giving you IV fluids to fix that. You’ll feel better soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. What about the breathing? I was breathing so fast.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s called Kussmaul breathing. Your body was trying to blow off acid to balance your blood. It’s improving now that we’re treating the DKA.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know that had a name.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We also put in a central line in your neck for better access. It helps us give meds and fluids safely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It feels weird, but I don’t mind. Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and a chest X-ray confirmed it’s in the right place. Your lungs look clear—no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I’ve had a cough, but everyone at home is sick with a cold.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely a viral URI. We gave you antibiotics just in case, but your urine test didn’t show infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ve been in outpatient treatment for alcohol. I haven’t had a drink in over two weeks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great to hear. We’re giving you thiamine and multivitamins to support that. Your CIWA score is low, so no withdrawal signs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Your blood sugar is down to 180, and your acid levels are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. Can I eat something?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re starting you on a regular diet. We’ll switch from the insulin drip to your regular shots—Lantus in the morning and at bedtime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll keep that. The endocrine team reviewed your case and said to keep your Lantus dose the same but adjust the sliding scale if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. I’ll try not to miss doses again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to help. You’ve also been seen by psychiatry. They recommend continuing your venlafaxine and mirtazapine and following up with your therapist.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’ve been feeling better mentally, but stress still gets to me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s understandable. Managing diabetes is hard, especially with other challenges. We’ll make sure you have support.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing really well. Your labs this morning are almost all normal. Blood sugar 173, potassium 3.5, creatinine 0.7.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Can I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re discharging you today. One thing—your blood cultures showed a little bacteria, but it’s likely just skin contamination, not a real infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Should I worry?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, not at all. We’ll follow up if anything changes, but it’s very likely nothing. Just keep taking care of yourself.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I’ll follow up with my doctors and take my insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Call if your blood sugar goes above 300 or you feel sick again. Take care.
